# Decoding imagined speech from scalp EEG: a leakage-controlled benchmark on two public datasets

*Draft. Every number traces to a row in `results/LOG.md`; tables are regenerated by
`scripts/build_tables.py`. All planned experiments are complete.*

## Abstract

We ask how much of a five-word imagined-speech vocabulary can be decoded from non-invasive EEG
when evaluation is strict: no information crosses from test to training, chance is the binomial
threshold for the actual test size rather than 1/k, and within-subject, cross-session and
cross-subject results are reported separately. On BCI Competition 2020 Track 3 (15 participants,
five phrases), a Riemannian tangent-space classifier reaches 40.4% on the official test split
(chance threshold 22.4%; label-shuffle p = 0.0099), while two convolutional networks reach 25.7%
and 28.5%. The same classifier is at chance (19.9%, threshold 20.8%) when the test participant is
held out. On Nieto et al. 2022 (10 participants, four imagined words, three sessions) the same
classifier is at chance within subject, across sessions and across participants. A frequency-band
ablation locates the Track 3 effect in the 30-40 Hz band (0.443 alone, above every wideband
configuration), the range most exposed to muscle activity and one Track 3 cannot audit because it
records no muscle channel. Neither Euclidean Alignment nor cropped training helps: alignment leaves
cross-subject accuracy at chance, and cropping costs 2.8 points within subject.
We conclude that a reliable, person-specific, task-locked effect is detectable on one dataset, that
it does not transfer across people or reappear on a second dataset, and that its frequency profile
and the phrase-length pattern together argue against reading it as decoded imagined-speech content.

## 1. Introduction

Imagined speech, saying words silently with no movement, is an appealing BCI paradigm but a weak
EEG signal. Reported accuracies range from near chance to above 80% on the same datasets, and
recent leakage-controlled re-analyses attribute much of the spread to evaluation practice:
pooled sessions, crops of one trial on both sides of a split, preprocessing fitted on all data,
and comparison against 1/k with small test sets. This study sets out to measure the effect with
those failure modes closed, on public data, with every experiment logged.

Contributions: (1) an evaluation harness in which every split is checked for leakage and every
accuracy is paired with the exact-n binomial threshold and, for headline numbers, a label-shuffle
null; (2) a reproduction of published baselines on Track 3's official split; (3) the first
cross-session measurement on Nieto et al. 2022 under the same harness; and (4) an ablation over
frequency band, Euclidean Alignment and cropped training which locates the within-subject effect in
the band most exposed to muscle activity and argues against a speech-content interpretation.

## 2. Data

Two public datasets; full datasheets in `docs/DATASET_CARDS.md`.

- **BCI Competition 2020 Track 3.** 15 participants, five imagined phrases (Hello, Help me, Stop,
  Thank you, Yes), 64 channels at 256 Hz, one session each. Official split per participant:
  300 train, 50 validation, 50 test trials. We use the NEMAR BIDS copy, which includes the
  organisers' test labels.
- **Nieto et al. 2022 (inner speech).** 10 participants, four Spanish direction words, 128 channels,
  three sessions on separate days. We use the authors' preprocessed epochs and only the inner-speech
  condition (2,236 trials; 559 per class), 1.0-3.5 s after the cue.

## 3. Methods

**Preprocessing (fixed, per trial).** Average reference; 60 Hz notch for Track 3 (Nieto is
already notch-filtered by its authors); 4th-order Butterworth band-pass, applied forward and
backward; optional resampling to 128 Hz for the networks. Each trial is filtered on its own, so
no sample from one trial influences another.

**Models.** (a) Majority class. (b) Riemannian: OAS-shrunk spatial covariance, tangent-space
projection around the training-fold mean, logistic regression. (c) EEGNet and (d) ShallowConvNet
(braindecode), with per-channel scaling and early stopping computed from the training fold only.
(e) Riemannian with Euclidean Alignment: per-participant covariance whitening fitted on the
training fold; for an unseen participant the reference is computed from their own unlabelled
test trials (standard EA practice; stated wherever used).

**Protocols.** Within-subject on the official split (Track 3) or stratified 5-fold grouped by
trial (Nieto); cross-session: leave one session out (Nieto only); LOSO: leave one participant
out. Settings for Track 3 were chosen on train -> validation; each final configuration touched the
test split once.

**Statistics.** Chance threshold = Combrisson & Jerbi (2015) binomial 95th percentile for the
pooled test size; per-participant thresholds for per-participant claims; label-shuffle null
(labels permuted within participant, whole pipeline rerun) for headline numbers.

## 4. Results

### 4.1 Track 3, official split (within-subject)

| Model | Validation | Test | Participants above own threshold |
|---|---|---|---|
| Majority class | 0.200 | 0.200 | 0/15 |
| EEGNet | 0.233 | 0.257 | |
| ShallowConvNet | 0.240 | 0.285 | |
| Riemannian (0.5-30 Hz) | 0.415 | **0.404** | 12/15 |

Pooled threshold 0.224 (n = 750); shuffle null for the Riemannian model: mean 0.196, max 0.237
over 100 shuffles, p = 0.0099.

### 4.2 Track 3, cross-subject (LOSO)

Riemannian (0.5-30 Hz): **0.199** pooled over 6,000 trials, threshold 0.208, binomial p = 0.59;
0/15 participants above their own threshold (range 0.172-0.228). No shuffle test was run on a
chance-level result.

### 4.3 Nieto, three protocols (4 words, n = 2,236, threshold 0.265)

| Model | Within-subject | Cross-session | LOSO |
|---|---|---|---|
| Majority class | 0.249 | 0.250 | 0.250 |
| Riemannian (0.5-40 Hz) | 0.224 | 0.263 | 0.247 |
| ShallowConvNet | 0.235 | - | - |

No cell exceeds the threshold. Predictions are balanced across classes and per-participant
accuracies span 0.19-0.31, so the sub-1/k within-subject value is sampling noise, not a
classifier artefact. The cross-session result is the project's only measurement of day-to-day
transfer, and it is at chance.

### 4.4 Frequency-band ablation

One band at a time, Riemannian classifier, same protocols.

| Band | Track 3 train -> val | Track 3 LOSO | Nieto within | Nieto cross-session | Nieto LOSO |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1-8 Hz | 0.311 | 0.208 | 0.233 | 0.246 | 0.268 |
| 8-13 Hz | 0.291 | 0.197 | 0.251 | 0.275 | 0.230 |
| 13-30 Hz | 0.403 | 0.201 | 0.234 | 0.270 | 0.259 |
| **30-40 Hz** | **0.443** | 0.198 | 0.209 | 0.264 | 0.256 |
| 0.5-30 Hz (ref.) | 0.415 | 0.199 | - | - | - |
| 0.5-40 Hz (ref.) | 0.405 | - | 0.224 | 0.263 | 0.247 |

Thresholds: 0.224 (Track 3 val), 0.208 (Track 3 LOSO), 0.265 (Nieto). On Track 3 accuracy rises
monotonically with frequency and peaks in the highest band tested, which alone exceeds every
wideband configuration. On Nieto no band reaches the threshold in any protocol.

### 4.5 Euclidean Alignment

| Dataset | Protocol | Baseline | +EA | Threshold |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Track 3 | train -> val | 0.415 | 0.415 | 0.224 |
| Track 3 | LOSO | 0.199 | 0.204 | 0.208 |
| Nieto | within-subject | 0.224 | 0.224 | 0.265 |
| Nieto | cross-session | 0.263 | 0.263 | 0.265 |
| Nieto | LOSO | 0.247 | 0.237 | 0.265 |

EA leaves within-subject accuracy unchanged and does not lift either dataset above chance across
participants.

### 4.6 Cropped training

1 s windows every 0.5 s, all crops of a trial on one side of every split, majority vote per trial at
test time (so `n_test` counts trials, not windows).

| Dataset | Protocol | Baseline | +Crops | Threshold |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Track 3 | train -> val | 0.415 | 0.387 | 0.224 |
| Track 3 | LOSO | 0.199 | 0.200 | 0.208 |
| Nieto | within-subject | 0.224 | 0.239 | 0.265 |
| Nieto | cross-session | 0.263 | 0.271 | 0.265 |
| Nieto | LOSO | 0.247 | 0.242 | 0.265 |

Cropping lowers Track 3 within-subject accuracy by 2.8 points and leaves every other cell where it
was. Five times as many training examples did not compensate for shortening each from 3.1 s to 1 s.

## 5. Discussion

**A real but person-specific effect.** On Track 3 the within-subject result is far above the
shuffle null and reproduces independently on validation and test, yet the same features carry no
information across participants. The drop from 0.404 to 0.199 is the central finding.

**What the within-subject signal is, and is not.** The band ablation is the decisive result of this
study, and it is unfavourable to a speech interpretation. Accuracy rises with frequency and peaks
at 30-40 Hz (0.443), the band most exposed to facial, jaw and neck muscle activity, above every
wideband configuration we ran. Cortical correlates of speech imagery are usually reported in lower
bands; a profile that climbs into the EMG range is the signature of muscle contamination, and Track 3
records no muscle channel with which to test or remove it. An earlier observation of ours pointed the
same way: cutting the band at 30 Hz did not reduce accuracy, which we first read as reassurance, but
the per-band results show the lower bands simply carry a weaker version of the same effect
(0.31 and 0.29) rather than the whole of it.

Phrase length points the same direction: "Help me" and "Thank you" were recognised best and "Stop"
worst, consistent with a model detecting the duration or rhythm of an articulatory act rather than
which word was imagined. We therefore report the Track 3 within-subject number as a reliable,
person-specific, task-locked effect, and explicitly not as evidence that imagined-speech content was
decoded.

**Cropping points the same way.** Cutting trials into 1 s windows cost 2.8 points within subject
(0.415 -> 0.387) despite five times the training examples. A representation that distinguished word
identity moment to moment should tolerate shorter windows; one that tracks the duration or rhythm of
an articulatory act should not, because cropping destroys exactly that structure. Together with the
frequency profile and the phrase-length pattern, this is a third line of evidence pointing away from
word-identity decoding.

**Alignment does not transfer what is not shared.** Euclidean Alignment, which buys several points of
cross-subject accuracy on motor imagery, changes nothing here (Track 3 LOSO 0.199 -> 0.204, still
below threshold). Aligning coordinate frames can only help when a shared cross-subject pattern exists
to align; the LOSO results indicate there is none.

**Repeated cues.** Each cue was imagined four times and the public files do not identify which
trials share a cue. If the official split places repetitions on both sides, test accuracy is
optimistic. We cannot check this from the public data and flag it as a limitation.

**Comparison with published numbers.** The competition's 82.6% was not reproduced by us or by two
independent re-analyses; our ShallowConvNet validation accuracy (0.240) matches one of them
(0.244). Our Riemannian result is higher than their band-power models (0.31-0.33), plausibly
because full covariance captures more than band power on this montage; we report it with its null
rather than claim it as an advance.

## 6. Limitations and what we did not do

- Two datasets, 25 participants in total; no own recordings.
- Networks were trained on CPU with a fixed schedule; a wider search might change their ranking. The
  networks were evaluated within subject only; the cross-subject and cross-session claims rest on the
  Riemannian classifier, which was the strongest model wherever both were run.
- No per-participant embedding or contrastive model was attempted. Each needs repeated
  multi-hour network runs, which this project's single-CPU budget could not cover; the band ablation
  was prioritised instead, and it turned out to be the more informative experiment.
- Track 3's repeated-cue structure is unknown (see above).
- The muscle interpretation is an inference from the frequency profile, not a measurement. Only a
  recording with a simultaneous EMG channel could confirm or refute it; neither public dataset has one.
- Ablations were run on the validation split and LOSO, never on the Track 3 test split, which was
  touched once per model in Section 4.1 and not revisited.

## 7. Reproducibility

`python scripts/reproduce.py` reruns every experiment in this paper from a fresh clone in the
order listed; `python scripts/build_tables.py` regenerates the tables in this paper from
`results/LOG.md`. Seeds are fixed and the log records the commit of every run.

Verified on 2026-11-17: a fresh `git clone` of this repository, with the datasets downloaded by
`scripts/download_data.py`, passes the full test suite (71 tests; the 2 real-data loader tests skip
when `data/` is absent, since data is never committed). Runtimes on one laptop CPU, for planning:
Riemannian runs take minutes to ~1 h per protocol; each neural-network run takes 8-12 h; the
Track 3 LOSO permutation test with 20 shuffles exceeded 8 h and was not used (a chance-level result
needs no shuffle null).
